clue.text: Peter starts the New Year with a riotous party — grand fellow !

indicators.note: Peter starts the run, standing first before the other pieces

parts.note: Peter Pan, so Peter gives his surname
January opens the new year, abbreviated Jan
a drum was an old word for a noisy, crowded evening party or rout

explanation.surface: A man called Peter kicks off January with a wild party, and is a splendid chap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' places PAN at the head, before JAN and DRUM. DRUM in the sense of a tumultuous party is an old (18th-century) usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandee who thinks himself very important, a pompous official, from Samuel Foote's nonsense title 'the Grand Panjandrum'.

clue.text: Pretty edgy, the company in hell

indicators.note: the company sits inside the word for hell

parts.note: the pit is a name for hell
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Rather nervous, the firm going through hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty edgy' looks like 'rather nervous', but means forming a decorative edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A picot is a small loop of thread used as an ornamental border on lace or ribbon.

clue.text: Answer that makes the heart grow fonder?

definitions.text: Answer that makes the heart grow fonder?

parts.words: Answer that makes the heart grow fonder?
parts.note: absence makes the heart grow fonder, so this is the reply given at the door when someone is absent

explanation.surface: What reply wins someone's affection?
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'absence makes the heart grow fonder'; the reply a servant gives a caller when the householder is out signals absence.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the polite answer at the door that the person sought is away.

clue.text: Possible cause of a strike of fruit-pickers

definitions.text: Possible cause of a strike of fruit-pickers

parts.words: Possible cause of a strike of fruit-pickers
parts.note: a dispute among pickers could come from a quarrelsome piece of fruit, the golden prize of Greek myth

explanation.surface: Why orchard workers might walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Eris threw a golden fruit marked 'for the fairest' among the goddesses, causing the dispute that led to the Trojan War.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden fruit thrown by Eris, the source of strife, is a byword for anything causing a dispute.

clue.text: College for future ministers ?

parts.note: a Cambridge college shares its name with the London street where the Prime Minister lives

explanation.surface: A seminary training men for the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ministers' suggests clergy; here it means government ministers, who live in a London street of the same name as a Cambridge college.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cambridge college bears the name of the Westminster street home to the Prime Minister and Chancellor.

clue.text: Square deal piano

explanation.surface: A fair price on a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square deal' reads as fair dealing, which is being honest; the second sense is the vertical domestic piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone honest deals squarely, and an instrument with vertical strings is the standard household kind of piano.

clue.text: All your —— are queens, said Florizel to Perdita

definitions.text: All your —— are queens, said Florizel to Perdita

parts.words: All your —— are queens, said Florizel to Perdita
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from The Winter's Tale, where the prince praises everything the shepherdess does as queenly

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare: Prince Florizel tells Perdita that all her doings are fit for a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Winter's Tale (Act 4) Florizel says to Perdita, 'each your doing ... crowns what you are doing in the present deeds, that all your acts are queens'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is deeds or doings, the plural of a deed, completing Florizel's line of praise.

clue.text: About the wheatear-a bird a little way off

indicators.note: off means taken away, so the short distance is removed from the bird

parts.note: the chaffinch is a common finch
an inch is a short distance

explanation.surface: Concerning the wheatear, a bird seen at a little distance.
explanation.walkthrough: The wheatear is also a bird, which misleads; here 'wheat ear' is the head of grain, and the husk around it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The husks threshed from grain are what surround each ear of wheat.

clue.text: " Lion " brand honey

parts.note: Samson found bees and honey in a lion's carcass, and his riddle said out of the strong came forth this quality

explanation.surface: A jar of honey sold under a lion trade mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson's riddle (Judges 14): 'out of the strong came forth sweetness'; the lion and bees appear on tins of Lyle's Golden Syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: Honey is sugary, and the riddle names the quality that came from the lion.

clue.text: Vain so to try to make the desert blossom as the rose

definitions.text: Vain so to try to make the desert blossom as the rose

parts.words: Vain so to try to make the desert blossom as the rose
parts.note: Isaiah promises the desert shall blossom as the rose; to try it by farming would be wasted labour

explanation.surface: It is futile to try to make the wilderness flower.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to labour fruitlessly; the clue pictures literal tilling of a desert, echoing Isaiah 35.
explanation.definitionFit: Working dry dunes with a farm blade is the idiom for pointless toil.

clue.text: Enough wind to stop a mouse

explanation.surface: Just enough of a breeze to halt a small rodent in its tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: a feline's paw stops a mouse. The first is the sailor's term for a puff of wind ruffling the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A light breeze just enough to ripple calm water is named after a feline foot, and that foot is also what pins down a rodent.

clue.text: Paradoxically the order of it was for hanging

definitions.text: Paradoxically the order of it was for hanging

parts.words: Paradoxically the order of it was for hanging
parts.note: the hangman's order to pull the lever that frees the trapdoor is, oddly, a command to set something free

explanation.surface: A puzzling execution: the command given meant a man would hang.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox: at a hanging the fatal instruction is to let go the drop, so freeing the trap is what kills.
explanation.definitionFit: Letting go of the trap door frees it, and freeing or letting go is the plain meaning of the word.

clue.text: Uttering 22

parts.note: 22 down is a little laughing noise, so uttering it means giggling

explanation.surface: Saying the answer to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 22 down is the sound of a suppressed giggle, so saying it is laughing in a half-hidden way.
explanation.definitionFit: Giggling nervously or in a suppressed way is making that small laughing sound.

clue.text: Fu Tin is indisposed

indicators.note: indisposed means out of order, so the letters of the name are put out of order

explanation.surface: A man named Fu Tin is feeling poorly today.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'indisposed' rearranges FU TIN, and a man who is indisposed is in poor health.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unwell or out of condition is what it means to be indisposed.

clue.text: Send back the works of the phoney

indicators.note: sending something back returns it, so the word for the works is read backwards

parts.note: works are opuses, abbreviated op., plural ops
taken as written

explanation.surface: Return the creative works of the impostor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send back' turns OPS into SPO, and OF follows as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoof is a hoax or parody, so as an adjective it means sham or fake.

clue.text: Student hailed by still in insatiate Cerberus?

parts.note: a sop to Cerberus is the bribe thrown to the hungry three-headed dog guarding Hades
ho is a call to hail someone
still in the sense of yet more

explanation.surface: A student is greeted by the ever-hungry hound of Hades.
explanation.walkthrough: A sophomore is a second-year student, chiefly in the US; Cerberus is pictured crying 'ho, more!' after his sop.
explanation.definitionFit: A second-year undergraduate or high-school pupil in America.

clue.text: Fleet Lodge, Kirkcudbrightshire

parts.note: a lodge at an estate entrance, and also the first word of a small town in Kirkcudbrightshire whose name ends 'of Fleet'

explanation.surface: An address: a lodge called Fleet, in the south-west of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Kirkcudbrightshire was a county in south-west Scotland; one of its towns is Gatehouse of Fleet. 'Lodge' is the other sense: a porter's house at a gate.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodge at the entrance to a park or estate is the porter's house by the gate, and the word also starts the Scottish town's name.

clue.text: Incorrectly assess submarine knots

parts.note: submarine means under the sea
knots measure speed, a rate of travel

explanation.surface: Misjudging how fast a submarine is going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incorrectly' looks like an anagram signal; it is part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To value something too low is one way to misjudge it.

clue.text: Looking ahead to quiet work before the exam

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet
students do revision before a test, going over what they learned

explanation.surface: A student planning sensibly to study quietly before a test.
explanation.definitionFit: Foresight, seeing a thing before it happens, is what looking ahead amounts to.

clue.text: What makes a trencherman trenchant

parts.note: a hearty eater cuts his food with his front cutting teeth, so they make him sharp or cutting

explanation.surface: What makes a hearty eater sharp in his remarks?
explanation.walkthrough: A trencherman is a hearty eater; 'trenchant' means cutting, and his front cutting teeth do the cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp front tooth used for biting and cutting food.

clue.text: It won't go under if you shoot it, on the contrary

definitions.text: It won't go under if you shoot it, on the contrary

parts.words: It won't go under if you shoot it, on the contrary
parts.note: a target shot goes under, but anyone who shoots these falls, riding them in a barrel, is the one likely to go under

explanation.surface: A thing that will not sink when you fire at it.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'shoot' rapids or falls is to ride over them; the North American falls stay put, and it is the person shooting them who goes under.
explanation.definitionFit: The great falls on the US-Canada border, famous for daredevils going over in barrels.

clue.text: Shady haunt

parts.note: the underworld of Greek myth is where the ..., spirits of the dead, dwell

explanation.surface: A dim, shaded spot where someone likes to hang out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady' looks like 'shaded' or 'dubious'; here it means 'of the shades', the ghosts of the dead in Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek underworld is the home that ghosts frequent, a place of the departed spirits.

clue.text: One of three in threading a needle ?

definitions.text: One of three in threading a needle

parts.words: One of three in threading a needle
parts.note: threading a needle involves the needle's eye and the two eyes of the person doing it

explanation.surface: A sewing puzzle: what three things take part when you thread a needle?
explanation.walkthrough: The three are the needle's eye and your own two eyes; the answer is another word for an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye is the organ of sight, and the word also names an eyepiece or lens.

clue.text: He's in place of the driver to someone's amusement

indicators.note: the clue's he is placed inside the golfer's starting point

parts.note: a golfer uses a driver club from the tee
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man takes the driver's seat, much to someone's amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driver' suggests a motorist; here it is the golf club used off the tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A suppressed giggle, the sound someone makes when amused.

clue.text: Generous father figure with liberal art backing in privacy

parts.note: Santa Claus, Father Christmas, the gift-giver

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so liberal and art are read from the back

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A kindly patriarch who supports the liberal arts behind closed doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns L + ART into TRAL, placed after CLAUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Claustral means cloistered, like life in a monastery, secluded from the world.

clue.text: Hark ! Hear him rhapsodize

indicators.note: hear means we take the word for hark by its sound

parts.note: list is an old word meaning listen, like hark

explanation.surface: Listen! Hear the man speaking in ecstatic praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hungarian composer wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies, so 'him rhapsodize' points to him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hungarian pianist-composer famous for his Hungarian Rhapsodies for piano.

clue.text: Stockjobbers

parts.note: read as people whose job is with stock, that is livestock, not stock-exchange dealers

explanation.surface: Dealers on the stock exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: A stockjobber was a London stock-exchange dealer; here the word is read as workers who tend livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle herders are people whose job is minding the animals called stock.

clue.text: Unregenerate Flora

parts.note: plants that do not come back after their one season, read as a stubbornly unreformed woman named Flora

explanation.surface: A woman called Flora who refuses to mend her ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unregenerate' usually means unreformed, and Flora looks like a name; here they mean garden plants that do not regrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that complete their life cycle in one year and must be sown again do not regenerate.

clue.text: Were in jug

indicators.note: the letters of were are put in the jug and come out jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Some people were locked up in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jug' is slang for prison, so the surface reads as people in jail; the letters of WERE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A large water pitcher, as used with a basin on an old washstand.

clue.text: "Ballad of the Great Bed of Ware "?

definitions.text: Ballad of the Great Bed of Ware

parts.words: Ballad of the Great Bed of Ware
parts.note: a ballad was printed on a large single sheet, and the enormous Great Bed of Ware would need a very wide bed sheet

explanation.surface: The title of an old song about a famous giant bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Great Bed of Ware is a famous oversized Elizabethan bed now in the V&A in London; it would need a very wide sheet, and old ballads were printed on single large sheets.
explanation.definitionFit: A large single printed page, as old ballads were sold, is literally a wide bed linen.
